pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten → Year 1). REPRESENTING NUMBERS multiple ways — with objects, pictures (dots/tallies), and on the NUMBER LINE — and moving between them. A REPRESENTATIONAL topic: the same quantity has many faces and fluency is translating among them. Underpins the concrete–pictorial–abstract (CPA) progression.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line'. Extends to Year 2/3 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.3 'Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0–20'. The number-line representation is developed in Grade 1 (1.NBT) and formalised as a number-line diagram in Grade 2 (2.MD.6).
• Operational details: Follow concrete → pictorial → abstract — show a number with counters/cubes/fingers, then draw it (dots, tallies), then locate/mark it on a number line and match to the numeral, keeping the faces side by side. Stress that every face means the SAME quantity. The number line is the pivotal (ordered, spatial, measured) and hardest representation — start with a numbered TRACK (discrete squares) before an empty LINE, and a marked line before a blank one.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (4–5) shows a given number (≤10) with objects/fingers and draws a matching picture. Tier B (5–6) locates a number on a marked 0–20 line and matches object/picture/numeral for the same value. Tier C (6) moves fluently between all four (object ↔ picture ↔ number line ↔ numeral) and explains they are the same amount.
bestPractices: Teach concrete → pictorial → abstract explicitly (CPA): objects, then drawings, then numeral + number line, kept side by side so the links are seen.
Introduce the number line via a numbered TRACK (discrete squares) before a continuous line; a marked line before a blank one.
Always tie every representation back to the quantity ('these all show five') so representations don't become disconnected rituals.
Use varied pictorial forms (dots, tallies, ten-frames) so the child abstracts 'fiveness' from the arrangement rather than a single picture.
Have children CREATE representations, not just read them — draw five, place five on the line, build five with cubes.
keyRepresentations: Number track (numbered squares) → number line (marked → blank).
The numeral card (abstract) linked to all of the above.
commonMisconceptions: Treating each representation as a separate task rather than the same quantity in different clothes.
Number-line errors: starting at 1 not 0, or counting the marks/gaps incorrectly; treating the line as a picture rather than a measured, ordered scale (the early 'number-line-as-picture' seed).
Drawing an inexact picture or miscounting tallies so the pictorial doesn't match the quantity.
Believing the numeral is 'the real number' and objects/pictures are not (or vice versa).

learn.summary: For ages 4–6, help children represent the same small quantity (to 20) in multiple ways — concrete objects (counters/cubes/fingers), pictures (dots, tallies, ten-frames), on a number line, and as a numeral — and translate fluently between them, grasping that every face means the SAME amount. Follow concrete → pictorial → abstract (CPA): show, then draw, then locate on the line and match the numeral, keeping the faces side by side. Introduce the number line via a numbered TRACK of discrete squares before a continuous line, and a marked line before a blank one. Have children CREATE representations, not just read them.

activities.title: Five shown four ways, driven from any face
feedback: When the child adds a counter but expects the numeral to stay, show all four faces updating together and ask 'what is the same about all of these now?'

If the child drives from the number line and is surprised the counters change, replay slowly and name the direction they actually moved: for example, 'you moved the marker one step up — so the amount went up by one everywhere' (or 'one step back — so it went down by one everywhere').
Praise naming the shared quantity ('five') rather than just completing the drag.
activities.rationale: Linked, synchronised representations driven from any panel make the CPA bridge something the child causes, countering the misconception that each representation is a separate task. Optional interaction examples (drag a counter, move the marker, live re-forming of the other panels) make the shared-quantity idea concrete; these are illustrative, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line'; Years 2–3 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
The concrete–pictorial–abstract (CPA) progression and multiple linked representations build number sense; the number line is a key structural representation introduced via a numbered track.
learnerActions: Set a small number (to 20) and see it at once as counters, a dotty picture (or tally/ten-frame), a point on a number line, and the numeral card.
Add or remove one counter and watch the picture gain or lose a dot, the number-line marker move one step, and the numeral change to match.
Drive the change from a DIFFERENT face: slide the number-line marker, or add a tally, and watch the other three faces re-form to match.
Say aloud 'these all show ___' each time, naming the quantity after a change.
Switch the number line between numbered-track mode (discrete squares) and continuous-line mode, and between a marked line and a blank one.
activities.intendedInsight: A quantity has many faces — blocks, dots, a spot on the line, a symbol — and when the amount changes, every face must change to match, because they all show the same amount in different clothing.

activities.title: Build it, draw it, place it (child creates every face)
feedback: If the drawn picture has the wrong count, draw and count together, one mark per count word, then lay the drawn marks beside the counters to check they match.
If the child writes the digit shape when asked to draw the quantity, point out 'the symbol tells us the number, but a picture shows how many — draw that many dots.'

If the child can build with counters but stalls on the line, lay the counters ALONG the number line, one in each unit space starting from 0 (between 0 and 1, between 1 and 2, and so on), so the far end of the last counter lines up with the number's mark; then count the jumps from 0 to check.
activities.rationale: Creating representations (not only reading them) is a stated best practice and exposes the 'draw the symbol not the quantity' and 'can produce in one mode only' error patterns so they can be addressed.
sourceClaims: K.CC.3: 'Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0–20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).'

Year 1: 'identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line'; Years 2–3 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
learnerActions: Given a target number (≤10 for younger children, to 20 later), build it with counters or cubes — fingers work well for numbers up to ten.
Draw a matching picture — exactly that many dots or tally marks, one mark per count word.
Locate and mark the number on a number line, counting the JUMPS from 0 aloud.
Match the numeral card to the set, the picture, and the number-line point, saying they all show the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: The child can PRODUCE a quantity in every mode, not just recognise it, and sees that the picture and number-line point carry the amount just as the objects do.

activities.title: Read the dot: count the jumps from 0
feedback: If the child reads 6 as 5 or 7, hop a finger from 0 counting the jumps aloud, labelling 0 explicitly as the start, not 'one'.
Confirm: 'the dot is 6 steps on from 0, so it marks 6.'
Ask 'where would 7 be? how do you know?' to check the jump-counting generalises.
activities.rationale: Off-by-one errors come from counting ticks instead of the gaps between them, or treating 0 as the first count; counting jumps from a labelled 0 targets this directly. The number line is the ordered, spatial, measured representation and the hardest, so it is introduced via a numbered track and a marked line precedes a blank one.
sourceClaims: The concrete–pictorial–abstract (CPA) progression and multiple linked representations build number sense; the number line is a key structural representation introduced via a numbered track.
learnerActions: Look at a number line from 0 to 10 with a dot marked on 6; point to the dot and say what number it means and how you know.
Count the JUMPS from 0 aloud, hopping a finger from 0, rather than counting the ticks.
Point to 0 and say what 0 means here — the start, not a step.
Then show the same number with counters and draw a matching picture.
activities.intendedInsight: A number-line point is read by counting the steps from 0, which is the start and not itself a step; 0 anchors the measured, ordered scale.

activities.title: Reference wall and match checks
feedback: For a correct match, ask the child to justify: 'how do you know that one shows 5?'
When a tap-reveal names a face, prompt the child to find the same quantity in another face before moving on.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal reference and matching/placing tasks are a good naming and assessment layer across representations; they support recognition but on their own do not elicit the independent construction and translation that the build/draw/place activity provides.
learnerActions: Use a 'number shown four ways' reference the child can tap to name each face (tap the number-line point → 'five'; tap the tally → 'five').
Answer 'which shows 5?' matching tasks across objects, pictures, number line, and numeral.
Use a slider to place a number on the line, or draw a path to mark it.
Discuss probe questions: 'You drew 6 dots and here are 6 counters — how are they the same? how are they different?' and 'If I show you 4 fingers, can you put a dot on the line for that number?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to name and match each face is a useful naming/reference layer that supports, but does not replace, building and translating for oneself.

constraints: Keep all faces (objects, picture, number line, numeral) side by side and always tie each back to the quantity ('these all show five') so representations don't become disconnected rituals.
Introduce the number line via a numbered TRACK (discrete squares) before a continuous line, and a marked line before a blank one; the number line is the hardest, measured, ordered representation.
Use varied pictorial forms (dots, tallies, ten-frames) so the child abstracts 'fiveness' from the arrangement rather than memorising one picture.

Recognition-only tasks (tap-to-reveal, 'which shows 5?' matching) assess and name but do not by themselves show the child can independently construct or translate a quantity; pair them with build/draw/place work.

Tier the demand: 4–5 shows a number ≤10 with objects/fingers and draws a matching picture; 5–6 locates on a marked 0–20 line and matches object/picture/numeral; 6 moves fluently among all four and explains they are the same amount.

A static reference image cannot itself let the child create or translate a quantity, so use it as a companion rather than the main teaching activity — this is a scope note about that specific scaffold's affordance, not a claim that static images cannot teach.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 3D interactive 'poor' (claiming a third dimension 'contradicts the number line's flat nature and adds nothing') and a conversation 'poor' ('no persona value'). These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, so they are not asserted here; a flat multi-panel linker is simply well matched to this 2D representational task.

The source's 'the killer move' framing that a linker makes understanding inevitable ('something the child causes') is a design claim, not evidence of efficacy; retained as rationale for the design, not as proven effect.
One cited source (NCETM/CPA guidance) is marked unverified in the original row; treat its claim as legacy-confidence and do not upgrade it.

sourceClaims were scoped to claims that back each activity's teaching principle. The jump-counting off-by-one correction (activity 3) and the recognition-vs-construction scaffold limit (activity 4) are standard pedagogy but are NOT directly supported by any sources[].claim; activity 4 therefore uses [], and activity 3 cites only the NCETM number-line/track claim, which supports the marked-before-blank sequencing in its rationale but not the jump-counting correction itself.
Fingers were explicitly scoped to numbers up to ten in the build activity, since they cannot represent values up to 20.

probeDeeper: You drew 6 dots and here are 6 counters — how are they the same? How are they different?
Where would 7 be on the line? How do you know?
If I show you 4 fingers, can you put a dot on the line for that number?
Point to 0 — what does 0 mean here?
assess.correctAnswer: The dot marks 6 — it's 6 steps on from 0. (Places/counts out exactly 6 counters.) (Draws 6 dots or tally marks.) Each way shows the same amount: six.

errorPatterns.pattern: number-line off-by-one — reads the marked point as 5 or 7 because they count the 0 tick as 'one', or count marks instead of the jumps between them
errorPatterns.nextMove: count the JUMPS from 0 aloud, hopping a finger from 0; label 0 explicitly as the start, not a step
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names the wrong number for the dot; starts the count at the 0 mark saying 'one'

errorPatterns.pattern: draws the symbol, not the quantity — asked to draw 6, writes the digit '6' or makes a vague scatter of marks rather than exactly six items
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw-and-count together, one mark per count word, then match the drawn set back to the 6 counters so the picture is seen to carry the amount
errorPatterns.revealedBy: the picture's count isn't 6, or the child draws the numeral shape

errorPatterns.pattern: can produce in one mode only — shows 6 counters fine but can't locate 6 on the line (or vice versa); treats each representation as a separate skill, not the same number
errorPatterns.nextMove: lay the counters ALONG the number line so position and quantity line up side by side, bridging the two representations — the quantity idea is there, only the link is missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: succeeds in one representation and stalls when asked to translate to another

responseLevels.gap: Translations don't preserve quantity — miscounts the number-line point, or draws the numeral / a wrong number of marks unrelated to the target.
responseLevels.full: Reads the marked point as the right number, produces the same quantity with counters and in a drawing, and explains that all three show the same amount.
responseLevels.partial: Represents the number correctly in one mode (e.g. counters) but falters translating to another — mislocates it on the line or is off-by-one — treating the representations as separate.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a number line from 0 to 10 with a dot marked on 6. Point to the dot and tell me what number it means and how you know. Now show me that same number using these counters. Last, draw me a picture that shows that number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the representations maps all three — number-line position, counters, drawing — to the same quantity, treating them as the same number in different clothes. A child without it mislocates the point (counts the 0 tick as 'one', giving 5 or 7), draws the numeral shape or a wrong number of marks, or produces counters unrelated to the target: the translations don't preserve quantity. Requiring both an INTERPRET (read the dot) and two TRANSLATES (counters, drawing) exposes exactly where the mapping breaks.
